The silhouette score reflects how well each cell fits within its assigned cluster relative to other clusters; higher scores represent more coherent clustering. Balanced KNN accuracy was computed using k=10. Each cell’s predicted label was inferred from a majority vote among its k-nearest neighbors in the PCA space (KNN accuracy). Balanced accuracy averages accuracies across all cell types, thus adjusting for label imbalance. Mean cLISI was used to quantify local label purity. For each cell, cLISI measures the diversity of neighboring cell types, with lower values indicating less label mixing and purer clusters. All metrics were calculated in the first 30 dimensions of the LSI space generated from the TF-IDF-normalized matrix using singular value decomposition (SVD).

We performed differential accessibility analysis to find differentially accessible regions in pDCs compared to other cell types. We used “FindMarkers” in the Signac package89 with test.use = “LR” and latent.vars=“peak_region_fragments” to perform differential analysis.

The PBMC-10k dataset was downloaded from the 10x Genomics website (https://support.10xgenomics.com/single-cell-multiome-atac-gex/datasets/1.0.0/pbmc_granulocyte_sorted_10k). We followed the processing steps outlined in the Seurat v5 vignette (https://satijalab.org/seurat/articles/seurat5_atacseq_integration_vignette). As this is a multi-omics dataset, we did not perform label transfer from scRNA-seq to scATAC-seq. Cell type labels were directly taken from the original dataset metadata. The pseudo-bulk peaks were also derived from the original dataset. We followed the same procedures used for the PBMC-8k dataset to conduct all downstream analyses.

The PBMC-48k dataset68 was downloaded from GEO (accession code GSE190992), containing paired scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq data. We processed the scATAC-seq data using the ArchR pipeline36, identifying 9.08% of cells as doublets using addDoubletScores and removing them with filterDoublets. For the scRNA-seq data, cells with predicted.celltype.l2.score > 0.9 were retained as high-confidence annotations. These cells were then used to transfer labels to scATAC-seq data via the addGeneIntegrationMatrix function in ArchR, which also provides a predictedScore for each assigned label. We selected 48,487 scATAC-seq cells with a predictedScore > 0.9 for downstream analyses, following the same procedures as for the PBMC-8k dataset. We found that cPeaks did not outperform other methods when doublets were not removed (Supplementary Fig. 5i), This observation emphasizes that rigorous data quality control is an essential step in ensuring the reliability of analyses.

Analysis of the CATLAS dataset for rare cell type discovery and analysis
The fragment file and metadata of CATLAS data were downloaded from http://catlas.org/catlas_downloads/humantissues/. We first analyzed GI epithelial cells from CATLAS5, constructing cell-by-feature matrices with 2000-bp genomic bins, cPeaks, cDHSs, CATLAS cCREs, and pseudo-bulk peaks, separately. For cPeaks, we used non-housekeeping cPeaks accessible in more than 50 cells as features. Pseudo-bulk peaks for GI epithelial cells were called using MACS2 with the parameters --shift 0 --nomodel --call-summits --nolambda --keep-dup all. Each matrix was preprocessed using the same steps applied to PBMC-8k, followed by graph-based clustering and UMAP visualization across dimensions 2 to 30. The evaluation of clustering performance was the same as PBMC-8k.

For the analysis of the whole CATLAS, we imported 92 fragment files from CATLAS into snapATAC271. Using the barcodes in the metadata download from http://catlas.org/catlas_downloads/humantissues/fragment/, we got 615,998 cells. Batch correction was performed using the “snapatac2.pp.mnc_correct” function. We used the “snapatac2.pp.select_features” function to select 500,000 features. We reduced the dimensions to 30 through the “snapatac2.tl.spectral” function and generated a neighbor graph through “snapatac2.pp.knn”. UMAP visualization was carried out using the “snapatac2.tl.umap” function. Adjusting the resolution parameter in “snapatac2.tl.leiden”, we identified either 30 or 111 cell clusters.

We calculated the proportion of each of the 111 cell types annotated in the CATLAS paper5. Depending on the ratio, we categorized cell types into three parts, each with 37 cell types. Based on the ranking of cell proportions, we evenly divided these cell types into three groups, with 37 cell types in each group. We sampled 50% from the whole dataset for 10 times, and calculated AMI, ARI, and H for each group, using the 111 cell type labels as ground truth, to evaluate clustering performance.

Analysis of the development datasets
We retrieved the fragment files and metadata for the retinal fetal dataset34 from GEO (accession code GSE184386) and processed the data following the filtering steps outlined in the original study. The generation of cell-by-feature matrices, clustering, and visualizations were conducted using the same methodology as applied to the PBMC dataset analysis. Cell labeling was based on the provided metadata, and all analyses were performed independently for each sample.

To quantify the well-positioned-cPeak ratio in all accessible cPeaks, we first binarized the cell-by-feature matrices, and then computed the normalized accessibility of all well-positioned cPeaks which is defined as the number of accessible well-positioned cPeaks divided by the total number of well-positioned cPeaks. To visualize the relationship between pseudotime and the well-positioned-cPeak ratio, we performed outlier filtering based on pseudotime values within each cell type cluster. Specifically, cells with pseudotime values below Q1−1.5×IQR or above Q3+1.5×IQR were identified as outliers and removed, where Q1 and Q3 denote the first and third quartiles of pseudotime, respectively, and IQR=Q3−Q1. This IQR-based filtering ensured a robust fit by reducing the influence of extreme pseudotime values. We then plotted the well-positioned-cPeak ratio along pseudotime using a smoothed curve fitted by a generalized additive model, using the default settings of the geom_smooth function in the ggplot2 R package.

We downloaded the human fetal cell atlas data26 from http://catlas.org/catlas_downloads/humantissues/fragment/. The analysis of these data followed the procedure as that of CATLAS data. For visualization, we used the UMAP coordinates provided in the supplementary files of the CATLAS paper5, allowing us to directly map and compare the well-positioned-cPeak ratios across fetal and adult cell types in a consistent embedding space.

Analysis of the tumor datasets
We downloaded the fragment files and metadata for the gynecologic malignancy dataset35 from GEO (accession code GSE173682). Cells from all 11 patients were combined to generate a unified cell-by-feature matrix. We followed the preprocessing steps in the original study to filter cells. We downloaded the fragment files and metadata for the hepatocellular carcinoma dataset69 from GEO (accession code GSE227265). We selected all samples diagnosed with hepatocellular carcinoma that contained more than 50 malignant cells. Malignant cells from these samples were then combined to construct a unified cell-by-feature matrix.

The generation of the cell-by-feature matrix, clustering, and visualizations were performed using the same methodology as applied to the PBMC dataset analysis. We labeled each cell using labels from the metadata file. The calculation of the well-positioned-cPeak ratio was performed using the same methodology as applied to the retinal fetal dataset.

The resources for cPeaks
The resource for cPeaks includes basic information and cPeak annotation, organized into 14 columns:
- ID: A unique 13-character string representing each cPeak, starting with “CP”, followed by “HS” (human), and ending with a nine-digit number. For example, the first cPeak is encoded as “CPHS000000001”.
- source: Indicates the origin of the cPeak, either “observed” or “predicted”.
- chr_hg38: The chromosome where this cPeak is located in the hg38 reference genome.
- start_hg38: The start position of this cPeak in the hg38 reference genome.
- end_hg38: The end position of this cPeak in the hg38 reference genome.
- housekeeping: Specifies whether the cPeak is accessible across nearly all datasets (“TRUE” or “FALSE”).
- shape_pattern: The shape pattern of the cPeak, categorized as “well-positioned”, “asymmetrically-positioned”, or “weakly-positioned”.
- inferredElements: The inferred regulatory elements associated with the cPeak, such as “CTCF”, “TES”, “TSS”, “Enhancer” or “Promoter”.
- chr_hg19: The chromosome where this cPeak locates in the hg19 reference genome.
- start_hg19: The start position of this cPeak in the hg19 reference genome.
- end_hg19: The end position of this cPeak in the hg19 reference genome.
- cDHS_ID: The ID of the overlapped cDHS region in the hg38 reference, formatted as “chr_start_end”.
- CATLAS_ID: The ID of the overlapped CATLAS cCREs region in the hg38 reference, formatted as “chr_start_end”.
- ReMap_ID: The ID of the overlapped ReMap region in the hg38 reference, formatted as “chr_start_end”.

We provide the complete list of cPeaks in https://mengqiuchen.github.io/cPeaks/Tutorials and https://zenodo.org/records/1779936791. In addition, we offer a dataset-level matrix recording the presence or absence of each cPeak across all datasets analyzed in this study, available at https://zenodo.org/records/17799367/files/cpeaks-by-dataset.tsv.gz. To further enhance usability for researchers interested in organ- or tissue-level analyses, we also aggregated this matrix by tissue type to generate a tissue-by-cPeak matrix, which is available at https://zenodo.org/records/17799367/files/cpeaks-by-tissue.tsv.gz. While they do not represent a comprehensive atlas of chromatin accessibility for all human tissues, they provide a practical and scalable reference for both biological interpretation and computational modeling.

All data analysis and visualization were performed using R (version 4.1.3) and Python (version 3.10). Schematic illustrations and final figure assembly and layout were completed using Adobe Illustrator 2024.

Statistics & Reproducibility
The sample size was determined by the number of samples included in the analyzed datasets. No selection or manual intervention was applied to samples. Statistical analyses were conducted using standard methods implemented in R version 4.1.3. We used two-sided statistical tests for all related analysis. The specific methods for statistic tests used are described in the corresponding sections of the Methods and figure legends.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
Meng et al developed a generic chromatin accessibility reference by aggregating peaks from 624 high-quality bulk ATAC-seq datasets, defining more than 1 million consensus peaks (cPeaks). They demonstrated cPeaks outperforms existing feature defining methods and references by improving cell annotation and rare cell type identification, and provide insights into chromatin dynamics during cellular differentiation and tumor progression. The collected large consortium of ATAC-seq would be a good resource in studying gene regulation. I have some comments as follows,
1. How the batch effect like ATAC-seq generated from different labs, protocols, etc are corrected before the integration?
2. For the developed CNN model is claimed to be modified based on scBasset. However, the difference and similarity of CNN and scBasset is unclear, and many technical details of CNN is missing. scBasset aims to predict the peaks for all cells in the single-cell setting, while the CNN is predict peaks for multiple tissues/organs. Please clarify this point and how the loss function is defined. Moreover, when the CNN performs zero-shot prediction, where training set does not include the tissue/organ/cell types in the testing set, please clarify the dimension of output labels in the training set and testing set as supervised learning need the same dimension of training and testing sets. Furthermore, are the training, validation and testing set split by different chromosomes? It is highly encouraged the detailed mathematical formula need to be present in the method section.
3. Further comments have for using cPeaks for facilitating the discovery and analysis of rare cell types with cPeaks or Investigating cell state transitions during development with cPeaks. It is unclear which peak set of CPeaks for the data analysis, tissue-matched for the single-cell data or all peaks? What is the peak overlap between scATAC peak-calling and the peak set provided by CPeaks in the data analysis? It is also unclear additional peak information provided by CPeaks with the same read information can achieve both tasks. In another word, what is the intuition to using the mapped reads from studied scATAC-seq data in a broad collection of peaks across more tissues and cell types, provided cPeaks, would improve the identification of rare cell types?
4. The github seems only provide the pipeline and software code. Would the CPeak data resources (peaks across all tissues/organs) can be provided in a format of online database as well as standard-alone download package? This will facilitate the users from both biology background and computational modeling.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
This manuscript presents cPeaks, a reference list of chromatin-accessible regions created by merging peaks from 624 bulk ATAC-seq datasets. The authors aim to provide a shared peak set for scATAC-seq analysis and employ a deep learning model trained on DNA sequence to predict additional peaks in unobserved tissues or cell types. While the study addresses an important challenge in the field, it has three major limitations. First, the cPeak list is not tissue- or cell-type-specific, which limits its applicability for studies requiring context-specific regulatory information. Second, using only DNA sequence to predict chromatin accessibility overlooks critical biological factors such as transcription factor binding and chromatin context, raising doubts about the validity of the predicted peaks. Third, the CNN model is trained on data from known tissues, and it remains unclear how it can reliably predict peaks in tissues it has not encountered during training. The detailed comments are as below.
Major Concerns
1. The cPeaks are derived by merging peaks identified using various peak-calling tools, each with different characteristics and sensitivities. This can introduce substantial technical variation. Although the authors report shape similarity across methods, the Pearson correlation coefficients range from 0.4 to 1.0, indicating inconsistency. The authors should clarify how they account for this heterogeneity and whether peak-calling parameters were harmonized prior to merging.
2. While the merged cPeaks serve as a universal reference, they may obscure important tissue- or cell-type-specific regulatory elements. Including annotations that flag cPeaks unique to specific contexts would enhance the utility of the resource. Alternatively, providing separate cPeak lists for each tissue or cell type would support more targeted and biologically meaningful analyses.
3. The deep learning model used to predict additional cPeaks is trained solely on DNA sequence, without considering key biological factors that influence chromatin accessibility, such as transcription factor binding, histone modifications, and chromatin context. As a result, it is unclear whether the predicted peaks truly capture cell-type-specific regulatory activity. Moreover, the model is trained on cPeaks derived from known tissues, yet the manuscript does not provide sufficient justification for its ability to generalize to unseen tissues. Finally, the prediction framework presents a potential circular logic issue: newly predicted peaks could be added to the shared peak list and used for further model training, allowing the process to expand indefinitely without clear stopping criteria or external validation. The authors should clarify how they prevent such iterative propagation of prediction error.
4. In benchmarking the coverage of scATAC-seq reads, the authors use MACS2-called peaks as ground truth. Since cPeaks may be partially derived from MACS2-called datasets, this could introduce bias in favor of cPeaks. Moreover, if MACS2 output is considered the gold standard, it raises the question of why not simply recommend MACS2-based peak calling per dataset. The authors should report the proportion of cPeak-contributing datasets that used MACS2. If MACS2 is dominant, it should be treated as a baseline method—like cDHS and CATLAS cCREs—rather than as the default reference. A side-by-side comparison of performance across all methods would be more appropriate.
5. The reliability of the curated cPeaks would be strengthened through validation with independent chromatin accessibility assays, such as ChIP-seq, CUT&RUN, or CUT&Tag. Such validation would help confirm that cPeaks represent biologically relevant regulatory elements.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
Summary
In this manuscript, the authors assembled 1.4 million observed consensus peaks (cPeaks) on chromatin openness from bulk ATAC-seq data in ENCODE and ATACdb and developed a deep CNN model to predict an additional 0.28 million cPeaks across the human genome. They further annotated the cPeaks and demonstrated utilities of the cPeaks in labeling scATAC-seq data, identifying “rare” cell types, investigating cell state transitions during development, and characterizing tumor cell subtypes. On the positive side, the topic is interesting, the assembled cPeaks can be a valuable resource to the field, and most Results sections are well written. On the negative side, crucial details are missing in Methods sections, some benchmarking analyses are neither thorough nor convincing, and some statements are over stretched. The manuscript needs a significant improvement.
Major concerns
1. The authors did not provide enough details on how Pearson correlation coefficient (PCC) is calculated. It can be easily misused and inflates similarity. What are the start and end points for PCC calculations when comparing two peaks? For example, comparing the peak in Fig. 1c with one shifting to the right by 250bp, how will the PCC be calculated? What is the PCC value?
2. Details on permutation tests need to be provided and the PCC distribution from 1000 permutations should be provided. Otherwise, Fig. 1d is not informative. The authors may want to convert the PCC values in Fig 1d to empirical p values, using the distribution from the permutation tests as the null distribution, and show the histogram of the empirical p values.
3. The similarity analysis should be performed on consensus peaks (cPeaks), not on multimodal peaks. Users care more about the end product than the intermediate results. Basically, the order between lines 120-126 and lines 104-119 should be switched.
4. Why is there no evidence for footprinting from transcription factor binding in Fig. 1c or Fig. 1f?
5. Fig. 4: This benchmarking analysis is very weak: a) The dataset of 2034 cells is very small and may miss complexities from more complicated datasets. The authors should include additional datasets generated from DOGMA-seq (Mimitou et al. 2021) and/or TEA-seq (Swanson et al. 2021) for benchmarking. b) The authors should provide more details on “clustering and annotation” (such as how many clusters and how many cell populations were used for benchmarking) and show a few examples of UMAPs.
6. The benchmarking on PBMC dataset in Fig. 5 is very problematic: a) The authors benchmarked against five different feature (peak) sets in Fig. 4, why did they limit it to pseudo-bulk peaks here? It is not obvious other feature sets won’t be able to identify the three “rare” cell types. b) There are much larger datasets in the literature with tens to hundreds of thousands of PBMCs. Why did the authors benchmarked on a small dataset of 8728 cells? c) Did they consider the existence of doublets? d) The “rare” cell types (pDC, DC, NK bright) are not that rare and are thus poor examples for “discovering” rare cell types.
7. The benchmarking on gastrointestinal (GI) epithelial cells in Fig. 5 is also problematic: a) Again, why did the authors limit the benchmarking to one feature set instead of five? b) The claim that “(p)seudo-bulk peaks in the original study failed to separate these subtypes” (lines 384-385) is not supported by the evidence in Fig. s5b. It is a purity issue, not a failure. c) It appears that there are impurities in the four rare cell types in Fig. 5h as well. The authors should quantify and compare impurity between methods. d) The improvements in Fig. 5i by cPeaks were small. Were they statistically meaningful?
8. The presentation on Fig. 6 can be improved: a) Similar analysis with respect to Fig. 6ab can be done with other feature sets. What is the novelty here? b) Lines 451-453: A scatter plot of pseudo-time versus well-positioned-cPeak ratio or a plot like Fig. 6d can be informative here. c) Lines 454-458: The presentation on the two datasets should be separated and mirror the analysis on the retinal data. As is, it feels rushed and incomplete.
9. Lines 483-488: Provide p values to assess significance.
Minor concerns
10. Lines 45-50: The literature review is incomplete. It ignores a different approach by a recent publication (Rachid Zaim et al. 2024).
11. In addition to Table S1-2, summary pie charts showing tissue and cell type compositions can be informative.
12. Fig. 1b: The curves grow linearly without reaching a plateau from 200 datasets. Descriptions should be accurate.
13. How representative is Fig. 1g or 1h? Can the authors provide similar results based on more datasets? As is, it is hard to know whether it is “cherry picking”.
14. The CNN model predicts cPeaks based on genome sequence regardless of tissue types. In other words, predicted cPeaks may not be open in specific tissues. The authors should distinguish testing prediction accuracy on known tissue-specific cPeaks from assigning predicted cPeaks as open to specific tissues. The latter is beyond the CNN model. The present description is ambiguous when claiming “that the CNN model can effectively predict missing cPeaks for previously unseen tissues or cell types”.
15. Fig. 3h: Remove the extra “the distribution of” from the legend.
16. Fig. S2b: Provide a legend.
17. Lines 369-370: The anchor method in Seurat has limitations in labeling scATAC-seq data. The authors are encouraged to explore newer methods for labeling scATAC-seq data in the literature.
18. It is unclear what is the difference between Fig. S5b and Fig. S5c. More details can be helpful.
19. Fig. 6 and Fig. S6: a) Lines 447-450: Results on enriched GO terms should be provided. b) A UMAP by life stage can be informative. c) All UMAPs should use the same projection and thus look similar and comparable.
20. Line 464: “Each box represents a single cell type …”. Did you mean each “line” here? How many total cell types were presented?
21. Line 479: It should be “Fig. 7b” not “Fig. 6b”.
22. Lines 489-494: These statements are stronger than what the evidence showed. The authors should weaken them to align with the evidence. Such statements also belong to Discussion, not Results.
23. Many readers may be interested in Table S4. It would be helpful to provide a brief description in Results (lines 508-512) and list it explicitly in Data Availability.
24. Line 846: There are 14 columns in Table S4, not 15 columns. This is also a good place to list Table S4.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_4: I co-reviewed this manuscript with one of the reviewers who provided the listed reports. This is part of the Nature Communications initiative to facilitate training in peer review and to provide appropriate recognition for Early Career Researchers who co-review manuscripts.

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
Responses to the Reviewer Comments
Reviewer #1
Comment 1-0
Meng et al developed a generic chromatin accessibility reference by aggregating peaks from 624 high-quality bulk ATAC-seq datasets, defining more than 1 million consensus peaks (cPeaks). They demonstrated cPeaks outperforms existing feature defining methods and references by improving cell annotation and rare cell type identification, and provide insights into chromatin dynamics during cellular differentiation and tumor progression. The collected large consortium of ATAC-seq would be a good resource in studying gene regulation. I have some comments as follows,
Reply:
Thank you so much for providing the excellent summary of our manuscript. We appreciate your feedback and have addressed all the points raised, as detailed in the responses below.
Comment 1-1
How the batch effect like ATAC-seq generated from different labs, protocols, etc are corrected before the integration?
Reply:
Thank you for the question. We have considered the potential batch effects in defining cPeaks. We apologize for not providing the relevant details in the previous version of the manuscript.
First, cPeaks are not derived from raw sequencing reads, which are indeed subject to batch-to-batch variability, but from pre-identified peaks that have already undergone peak calling within each dataset. This peak calling process effectively filters out substantial noise and retains biologically meaningful accessibility signals, thereby minimizing the influence of batch effects at the source.
We also evaluated the robustness of our approach by generating cPeaks separately from different batches. We have demonstrated that the shape profiles of merged peaks remain highly consistent across diverse experimental conditions. We observed strong concordance in peak shape across tissues of different origins, across sequencing technologies such as ATAC-seq and DNase-seq, and across different peak calling methods and parameters. These results suggest that the merged peaks represent intrinsic genomic features rather than artifacts driven by experimental variation.
In this revision, we reorganized the presentation of these results and added additional analyses, including the distributions of shuffled peak pairs and 250 bp–shifted peak pairs, to help readers better interpret the consistency and robustness of the peak shapes (Figure R1). We added the results in Line 119-141 and Figure 1d. We also expanded the discussion on this point in the revised manuscript to clarify the robustness of our method to batch effects (Line 144-148).
Figure R1 Correlations of peak shapes between different conditions.
Comment 1-2
For the developed CNN model is claimed to be modified based on scBasset. However, the difference and similarity of CNN and scBasset is unclear, and many technical details of CNN is missing. scBasset aims to predict the peaks for all cells in the single-cell setting, while the CNN is predict peaks for multiple tissues/organs. Please clarify this point and how the loss function is defined. Moreover, when the CNN performs zero-shot prediction, where training set does not include the tissue/organ/cell types in the testing set, please clarify the dimension of output labels in the training set and testing set as supervised learning need the same dimension of training and testing sets. Thank you for the question. We apologize for not providing a detailed description of the CNN model structure in previous manuscript.
scBasset aims to predict cell type-specific chromatin accessibility. Each output dimension in scBasset corresponds to number of cell types. In contrast, our goal is to predict the intrinsic chromatin accessibility potential of a genomic region. Rather than focusing on cell type- or tissue-specific accessibility patterns, we aim to identify a universal set of consensus peaks (cPeaks) shared across diverse biological contexts.
To achieve this, we modified the architecture of scBasset accordingly. We retained the core one-dimensional convolutional structure to capture DNA sequence patterns but simplified the output to a binary classification task. The model predicts whether a given genomic region corresponds to a cPeak or not. The output layer contains two dimensions representing probabilities of the two classes (cPeak / non-cPeak). We use the standard Binary Cross-Entropy Loss (BCELoss) as the training objective:

Comment 1-3
Further comments have for using cPeaks for facilitating the discovery and analysis of rare cell types with cPeaks or Investigating cell state transitions during development with cPeaks. Reply:
Thank you for the comment. We are sorry that the writing in the previous version of the manuscript caused misunderstandings regarding the usage of cPeaks. We would like to clarify this point as follows.
(1) Peak set used for analysis
We employed the complete set of cPeaks (observed cPeaks + predicted cPeaks), without restricting to tissue-matched or dataset-specific subsets in all analyses using cPeaks throughout this study, including the identification of rare cell types (e.g., Fig. 5) and the investigation of developmental transitions (e.g., Fig. 6). This is a key motivation for defining cPeaks in the first place: to establish a unified, high-confidence reference derived from diverse adult tissues, which enables researchers to map newly generated scATAC-seq reads directly to a common peak set. We added more detailed clarification in the revised manuscript (Line 260-261).
(2) Overlap with standard scATAC peak calling
We agree that the overlap between cPeaks and dataset-specific peaks is an important factor. We quantified this in two representative analyses. In the PBMC-8k analysis, MACS2-called pseudo-bulk peaks from all PBMCs totaled 133,648 peaks, of which 98.74% were covered by cPeaks. In the GI epithelial cell analysis, the fetal retina pseudo-bulk peak set contained 132,172 peaks, with 98.95% covered by cPeaks. These results indicate that cPeaks effectively encompass most accessible regions identified through conventional peak calling.
(3) Rationale for improved performance using cPeaks
The advantage of using cPeaks, particularly for analyzing rare cell types, lies in avoiding the limitations of pseudo-bulk peak calling. Traditional scATAC-seq analysis pipelines typically require aggregating cells into pseudo-bulk profiles before calling peaks. This step tends to overlook signals from rare cell types, as their accessibility patterns are often drowned out by more abundant populations and treated as noise. Accurately recovering such rare subtypes often requires iterative clustering and peak refinement.
In contrast, using cPeaks provides a comprehensive set of high-confidence potential accessible regions. We can quantify reads over a consistent reference from all cells, including rare subpopulations. This design avoids the information loss and bias introduced during dataset-specific peak calling, leading to improved resolution of rare cell types. In this revision, we revised the beginning of the relevant Results section to better highlight this motivation (Line 426-432).
Also, we added an additional benchmark analysis included in the revision, to support our explanation. Specifically, we constructed cell-by-feature matrices using five different references: cPeaks, cDHSs, CATLAS cCREs, 2,000-bp genomic bins, and pseudo-bulk peaks (called from the same dataset). We quantified clustering accuracy using five metrics, and cPeaks consistently achieved the best or second-best performance across all metrics (Figure R3). In addition, when transferring scRNA-seq labels to scATAC-seq data, cPeaks yielded higher prediction scores than all other references (Figure R4), further supporting their effectiveness in improving annotation quality. Furthermore, to assess the utility of cPeaks in downstream analyses, we examined differentially accessible regions identified using each reference set. Taking pDCs as an example, we compared their accessibility profiles to all other cells. We found that cPeaks enabled the identification of slightly more differentially accessible regions than cDHSs, and substantially more than CATLAS cCREs and pseudo-bulk peaks (Figure R5). All the results support the use of cPeaks for facilitating the analysis of rare cell types. These results are included in the revised manuscript (Line 440-462, Fig. 5b-c, Fig. S4c).
Thank you again for raising these points.

Comment 2-0

Reply:
Thank you very much for the comments. We would like to clarify the following:
(1) On context specificity: The main purpose of cPeaks is to provide a universal, robust reference set to support general scATAC-seq analysis. While not tissue-specific, cPeaks demonstrate strong performance across diverse datasets, including developmental and cancer contexts. Nevertheless, we now additionally provide tissue-level cPeak matrices to support context-aware analyses.
(2) On using only DNA sequence: Our CNN model is intentionally designed to predict the potential for chromatin accessibility based on intrinsic sequence features, not to capture context-dependent activity. As shown in our model interpretation (e.g., NeuronMotif analysis), the model captures biologically meaningful motifs.
(3) On prediction in unseen tissues: We evaluated the model’s generalization using held-out tissue-specific peaks as test sets and achieved high prediction performance. The model predicts whether a region could be accessible, but not in which tissue it will be so. We have clarified this in the revised manuscript. Also, the CNN predictions were not fed back into training, avoiding circular logic.
We appreciate your suggestions and have revised the manuscript to better clarify the design and intended use of cPeaks and the CNN model.
For detail, please see our point-by-point responses below.
Comment 2-1

Reply:
Thank for the comment. All cPeaks were derived from peaks identified using the same peak-calling tool, MACS2. Sorry that we didn’t write it clearly in previous manuscript, and we added the clarification in cPeak generation part.
For the report of shape similarity across methods, referring to Fig. 1d, we compared peak shapes generated by MACS2 (used in our pipeline) with those produced by CellRanger, to examine whether cPeak shapes are sensitive to the choice of peak-calling method. While some PCCs were relatively low, the overall median PCC remained around 0.665, indicating that cPeak shapes are generally stable across different algorithms. As we only evaluated a single sample produced by CellRanger, due to the limited number of cell types, the resulting merged peaks had relatively low resolution, which likely contributed to the lower observed PCC. Nevertheless, the shape similarity remained significantly higher than controls, supporting the robustness of peak shapes (Figure R6).
In addition, the ENCODE and ATACdb datasets were processed using different parameter settings of MACS2. We compared the cPeak shapes generated from these two sources and found high concordance, with a median PCC of 0.868 (Figure R6). Results show that cPeak shapes are largely robust to parameter variations within MACS2.
To improve clarity and reduce potential confusion, we revised the relevant descriptions in the manuscript (Line 110-141). Besides, we updated some words to explicitly state that all peaks used for generating cPeaks were called using MACS2 (Line 133-134). Moreover, we have split Fig. 1d into two parts (Figure R6): one showing comparisons internal to our pipeline (e.g., ENCODE vs. ATACdb with different MACS2 parameters), and the other showing external comparisons (e.g., MACS2 vs. CellRanger), to help readers better understand the robustness across different peak-calling methods.

Comment 2-3
The deep learning model used to predict additional cPeaks is trained solely on DNA sequence, without considering key biological factors that influence chromatin accessibility, such as transcription factor binding, histone modifications, and chromatin context. Reply:
Thank you for the comment. We apologize that our original description may have led to misunderstandings regarding the design and scope of our prediction framework. We clarify the following points as below:
(1) Considering key biological factors that influence chromatin accessibility
Our prediction task aims to identify genomic regions with an intrinsic potential for chromatin accessibility, rather than predicting accessibility status in specific cell types or tissues. While factors such as transcription factor binding, histone modifications, and chromatin context influence accessibility in a context-dependent manner, many accessibility patterns are encoded in the DNA sequence itself. Therefore, our deep learning model is intentionally based only on sequence features, which remain constant across conditions. Recent studies, such as DeepSEA and Enformer, have shown that some of these regulatory factors can, to a certain extent, be inferred from sequence. We thus believe that a well-trained CNN model can capture these patterns and accurately predict regions with the potential to become accessible.
In this revision, we further explored the interpretability of the CNN model using the NeuronMotif tool3 to identify sequence patterns that activate specific neurons in the network (Figure R7). By analyzing the last convolutional layer, we identified 342 TF motifs that could robustly activate at least one neuron. Notably, motifs from the bZIP family and CTCF/CTCFL were found to be highly influential across many neurons. These results suggest that the model has captured biologically meaningful features based on DNA sequence alone.
To improve clarity, we added a more explicit explanation of the model’s objective and underlying assumptions (Line 214-217). We also incorporated the model interpretation results into the revised manuscript (Line 250-254, Fig. S1h).

(2) Generalizing the model to unseen tissues
In the original manuscript, to evaluate the model’s ability to generalize to unobserved tissues or cell types, we conducted leave-one-context-out tests. We excluded cPeaks specific to a given tissue or cell type from the training set and used them as an independent test set. As shown in Figure 2c, the model was able to recover these held-out cPeaks with high performance, demonstrating its ability to learn general sequence features associated with chromatin accessibility from limited tissues.
We added further explanation of this evaluation strategy in the revised manuscript (line 229-236) to give a better explanation of the design of our generalization experiment.
(3) potential circular logic issue
We apologize that our previous description was unclear and caused misunderstanding. Our original framework did not involve any iterative expansion using CNN-predicted cPeaks. Specifically, we did not incorporate predicted peaks back into the training set at any stage. The CNN model was trained once using the observed cPeaks, and the prediction was performed in a single forward pass. To prevent misunderstanding, we have revised the manuscript to explicitly clarify this point (Line 793-795). Thank you again for helping us better present the design of deep-learning model.

Reply:
Thank you for the comment. We apologize for the lack of clarity in the manuscript, which led to a misunderstanding. All cPeaks were generated using MACS2. In the benchmarking experiment shown in Fig. 1h, we used peaks called by MACS2 on pseudo-bulk scATAC-seq data as a practical baseline. This strategy is the common practice in current scATAC-seq analysis pipelines.
Our goal in this experiment was to evaluate how well different predefined accessible region sets (cPeaks, cDHS, and CATLAS cCREs) recover accessibility signals in real scATAC-seq data, and thereby assess their utility as reference sets. To address your concern regarding potential bias, we examined the processing steps of each reference. All datasets used to generate cPeaks were indeed originally processed using MACS2, as were those used in the CATLAS cCREs. In contrast, the cDHS reference was derived using Hotspot2. We therefore believe the comparison is fair, as MACS2 was used across both cPeaks and CATLAS, and thus any advantage is not unique to cPeaks.
Furthermore, the MACS2-called pseudo-bulk peaks used as the comparison baseline in Fig. 1h were generated from an independent scATAC-seq dataset not used in cPeak construction. We found that cPeaks captured a similar proportion of reads as the MACS2 pseudo-bulk peaks, while substantially outperforming CATLAS cCREs and cDHSs. This suggests that cPeaks generalize well beyond the datasets used in their construction and provide a robust and comprehensive representation of accessible regions. We have clarified these points in the revised manuscript (Line 179-186, 681-683).
Lastly, we agree that for analyzing individual homogeneous datasets, MACS2 (or other conventional peak calling methods) is generally sufficient. However, our motivation for constructing cPeaks to facilitate large-scale integrative analysis across heterogeneous samples and improving performance in downstream analysis, such as rare cell detection. These advantages are demonstrated in the later benchmarking and case study sections of the manuscript.
Comment 2-5
The reliability of the curated cPeaks would be strengthened through validation with independent chromatin accessibility assays, such as ChIP-seq, CUT&RUN, or CUT&Tag. Such validation would help confirm that cPeaks represent biologically relevant regulatory elements.
Reply:
Thank you for this valuable suggestion. To assess whether cPeaks represent biologically meaningful regulatory elements, we validated their overlap with an independent ChIP-seq dataset from ReMap2022. Specifically, we downloaded the non-redundant ReMap peak set, and analyzed three pre-defined accessibility references: cPeaks, cDHS, and CATLAS cCREs, and calculated the proportion of ReMap peaks each covered. For each reference, we also generated a background peak set with matching peak length distribution and total peak number, excluding the original reference and ENCODE blacklist regions. Enrichment was assessed by comparing observed versus background overlap ratios.
Our results (Figure R8) showed that cPeaks covered 88.7% of ReMap peaks, slightly higher than cDHS (88.2%) and substantially more than CATLAS cCREs (72.9%). Relative to their respective background peak sets, the enrichment fold-changes were 13.5 (cPeaks), 7.2 (cDHS), and 8.4 (CATLAS), supporting the strong regulatory relevance of cPeaks.
To further assess specificity, we evaluated overlap between each reference and the individual TF ChIP-seq peak sets in ReMap. Among all the TFs evaluated, cPeaks showed greater coverage than cDHS for 54.8% of TFs, and greater coverage than CATLAS for 99.8% of TFs (Figure R9). On average, cPeaks covered 87.5% of TF peaks (median = 92.6%), slightly outperforming cDHS (mean = 87.0%, median = 92.0%) and clearly exceeding CATLAS (mean = 73.0%, median = 77.9%).
These results collectively support that cPeaks are highly enriched for biologically relevant regulatory regions and provide a more comprehensive representation than existing references.
We have revised the manuscript accordingly (Line 297-302, Figure S2a-b). Thank you again for your suggestion.

Comment 3-1

Reply:
Thank you for the suggestion. We apologize for the lack of clarity in our original description of the Pearson correlation coefficient (PCC) calculation. We provide a detailed clarification below and in revised manuscript regarding how PCC was calculated in our analysis, including the genomic window used and how shifts in peak position affect the correlation.
In our analysis, we calculated the PCC between two peak shapes using the genomic region defined by the merged peak boundaries from ENCODE as a fixed reference window. For any other peak set being compared, we aligned the signal within the same window. If the compared peak was shorter than the reference window, we padded the missing positions with zeros. If it extended beyond the reference window, we truncated the excess. This ensured that all comparisons were made over a consistent length and position.
Following your suggestion, we conducted an additional test to examine the impact of positional shifts. We introduced a 250 bp shift to peaks and recalculated the PCC values. The results, shown as green density plots in Figure R10, demonstrate that the PCC decreases under such shifts, as expected (We changed the violin plot in the original version to the density plot to better illustrate these distributions in limited space). This supports the sensitivity of our method to spatial misalignment and clarifies how PCC behaves under positional variation.

Comment 3-6
The benchmarking on PBMC dataset in Fig. 5 is very problematic: a) The authors benchmarked against five different feature (peak) sets in Fig. 4, why did they limit it to pseudo-bulk peaks here? It is not obvious other feature sets won’t be able to identify the three “rare” cell types. b) There are much larger datasets in the literature with tens to hundreds of thousands of PBMCs. Reply:
Thank you for the comments. We apologize for not including a more comprehensive benchmarking analysis and larger-scale PBMC data in the previous version of the manuscript. In the revised version, we have added the relevant experiments to address these concerns.
(a) Benchmarking with other feature sets
In the revision, we have extended the analysis to include additional reference sets (genomic bins, CATLAS cCREs, and cDHSs). We did not include the united peaks approach in this section, as it requires pseudo-bulk peak calling for each cell type using known labels. Such high-confidence ground truth labels are not available for these datasets, unlike the hematopoietic dataset used in our earlier benchmarking.
UMAP visualizations showed that most feature sets successfully resolved major cell types, including three rare subtypes: plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDCs), dendritic cells, and NK bright cells, each representing less than 1% of total cells (Figure R17). Genomic bins, however, failed to separate these rare subtypes. We then evaluated them using multiple clustering accuracy metrics (Calinski-Harabasz Index, Silhouette Score, cLISI, balanced KNN accuracy, and Davies-Bouldin Index), inspired by your Comment 3-7 (Figure R18). We also investigated the prediction scores when transferring scRNA-seq labels to scATAC-seq data (Figure R19). We calculated the number of differentially accessible regions of pDC cell type identified using each reference set and draw Venn plots (Figure R20). Compared to other reference sets, cPeaks enabled the identification of more differentially accessible regions (genomic bins were excluded from this comparison because they failed to cluster pDCs as a distinct population). In all these analyses, cPeaks outperformed other reference sets, supporting its utility in analyzing rare cell types. We added the results in Fig. 5b, 5c, S4b, S4c, and Line 433-453.
Figure R17 The UMAP plots of the dataset analyzed by each reference set.
Figure R18 Performance of clustering accuracy using different reference peak sets in the PBMC-8k dataset.
Figure R19 Distributions of the prediction scores of the cross-modality integration between the scRNA-seq data and scATAC-seq data analyzed with different reference sets. The prediction score reflects the confidence of predicted labels.
Figure R20 The Venn plot of the number of differential accessible regions calculated by cPeaks and other reference sets for pDCs.
(b) Benchmarking on larger datasets
In this study, we initially chose the 10X PBMC-8k dataset (8,728 cells) as it is widely used in benchmarking. To address concerns about dataset size and generalizability, we repeated the same analysis using a larger PBMC dataset from 10X Genomics (PBMC-10k, 10,412 cells). The results were consistent: cPeaks again ranked among the top in clustering accuracy metrics and enabled the identification of more differentially accessible regions compared to other references (Figure R21). These results support the robustness of cPeaks across datasets of different sizes and confirm that our findings are not limited to a specific small dataset. We added the results in Line 459-462 and the new Fig. S5.
Figure R21 Rare cell type discovery using cPeaks on the PBMC-10k dataset. (a) The proportion of each cell type in the dataset. (b) The UMAP plots of the dataset analyzed by each reference set. Each dot represented one cell. Different colors represented different clusters. (c) Performance of clustering accuracy using different reference peak sets. (d) The Venn plot of the number of differential accessible regions calculated by cPeaks and other reference sets for pDCs.
(c) Considering the existence of doublets
In our study, we followed quality control procedures to minimize their impact. Specifically, we excluded cells with an abnormally high total number of fragments, which are commonly indicative of doublets. This filtering step was applied prior to downstream analysis to reduce the presence of technical artifacts. Although we did not use a dedicated doublet detection algorithm, the resulting clusters showed clear separation and consistent label transfer from scRNA-seq, suggesting that any remaining doublets did not substantially affect our results. We have now added a clarification of this filtering criterion in the revised Methods section (Line 928).
(d) Issue of “rare” cell types
We apologize for not clearly stating the definition of “rare” in the previous version of the manuscript. We consider “rare” to refer to cell types that appear at low proportions within a given sequencing dataset. This definition may not correspond to biological rarity. The sampling bias or technical limitations in sequencing may also result in lower capture rates for certain cell types. The limited representation of these “rare” cells poses challenges for downstream analysis. For example, in the PBMC-8k dataset used in our analysis, pDC cells accounts for less than 2% of the total cells, and they cannot be well separated by genomic bins as reference, as shown in the new Fig. S4b. According to our definition, these cells fall within the category of rare cell types that are the focus of our analysis.
In the revised version, we retain the use of “rare” for consistency with common usage in the field but added explanation to more precisely define our intent (Line 427 and 487-489).
We thank you again for helping us to better clarify the definition of “rare” cells in our manuscript.

The purpose of evaluating the model on held-out, tissue- or cell-type-specific cPeaks was not to assign predicted peaks to specific tissues, but rather to test the model’s generalizability: whether it can recover potentially accessible regions that were not present in the training data. These regions, though observed in particular tissues, are treated in our analysis as sequence-defined elements whose accessibility may depend on cellular context.

General response to Reviewer #2

Following your suggestions, we have substantially revised the text, clarified methodological details, and added new analyses where appropriate. Comment 2-1. Clarification of Figure 1d and Peak Shape Similarity Analysis
The revised Figure 1d helps clarify the use of MACS2 and the overall strategy for generating cPeaks. I recommend that the authors provide additional detail on how the Pearson correlation was calculated. It would also be helpful to define the two negative control groups and the true peak group more clearly. Furthermore, I suggest avoiding the term “true peaks” when referring to the experimental group, since these peaks are still based on estimates from observed ATAC-seq or DNase-seq data and not experimentally validated ground truth.
Response:
Thank you for the helpful suggestions. To improve clarity, we have substantially revised the description of the peak shape similarity analysis in the Methods (lines 700–711). In the revised text, we describe how the genomic window was defined, how peaks were trimmed or zero-padded for alignment, and how base-pair-level values were used to calculate the PCC. We also provide clearer definitions of the two control groups. To further aid understanding, we added a new schematic (Figure R 1, or Fig. S1b in the revised manuscript) that illustrates the calculation procedure and the construction of the two control groups.
In addition, we replaced the term “true peak pairs” with “paired peaks” throughout the manuscript to avoid implying experimentally validated ground truth. We believe these revisions address your concerns and make the analysis more transparent and rigorous.
Figure R 1 Diagram of PCC computation and control group definitions.
Comment 2-2. Concern Regarding Potential Model Circularity
The authors appear to have misunderstood the original question regarding circularity. The concern is whether the current training process, which uses DNA sequence and cPeaks derived from observed ATAC-seq data, might predict novel peaks that are not included in the existing cPeak list. If those novel peaks were then added to the cPeak list and used to retrain the model, it is unclear whether this would result in further predictions of additional peaks. This raises the possibility of an iterative feedback process without a clear stopping criterion. The authors are encouraged to clarify whether such retraining was considered and whether this approach would be methodologically appropriate.
Response:
Thank you for further clarifying this question. Indeed, iteratively expanding the training set with model-predicted positives is a potential strategy explored in other contexts, such as positive-unlabeled (PU) learning. Following your suggestion, we evaluated whether such an iterative retraining approach could improve our model. Specifically, we added all predicted cPeaks (~0.28 million) to the training set and retrained the CNN. The updated model subsequently predicted an additional ~0.22 million peaks with scores above the threshold. Repeating this procedure led to the identification of progressively more peaks until nearly all candidate regions were classified as cPeaks, indicating uncontrolled expansion of predictions (Figure R 2). The results suggested a clear behavioral drift in the retrained model: with each iteration, the CNN increasingly classified nearly all candidate regions as positive. We hypothesize that this is likely due to the fixed-window prediction scheme used by the CNN, which does not provide precise peak boundary information. These results indicate that iterative retraining may propagate boundary noise and accumulate errors rather than improve model performance. Therefore, we consider the one-time training strategy adopted in this study to be the most appropriate and stable approach.
To help readers better understand this point, we have added a brief explanation in the revised manuscript (Lines 656–657, 803–805), noting that improving the prediction procedure to more accurately capture peak boundaries will be an important direction for future work.
Figure R 2 Number of newly/accumulated predicted cPeaks identified after each iteration of model retraining.
Comment 2-3. Benchmarking Comparison in Figure 1h
The comparison in Figure 1h may be affected by differences in the peak-calling tools used. Both cPeaks and CATLAS cCREs were generated using MACS2, but cDHSs were generated using Hotspot2. This makes it hard to tell whether the performance differences are due to biological signals or the choice of tool. Please clarify this point in the manuscript and consider discussing how tool differences may affect the results.
Response:
Thank you for the suggestion. We agree that the comparison in Figure 1h could potentially be influenced by differences in peak-calling algorithms, as cDHSs were originally generated with Hotspot2, whereas both cPeaks and CATLAS cCREs were produced using MACS2.
To directly address this concern, we attempted to reanalyse the data using Hotspot2 and perform comparison. However, despite our extensive technical efforts (including reimplementation of preprocessing scripts, setting computational environments on different servers, optimization of input data, and multiple recovery strategies), the analysis could not be completed successfully due to a fatal data-dependent bug in the core hotspot2_part1 module. This issue, which causes silent crashes even on validated datasets, reflects the fact that Hotspot2 has not been actively maintained for nearly a decade and is no longer compatible with nowadays computing environments.
We therefore approached the question conceptually. MACS2 is now commonly adopted as the default peak-calling tool for ATAC-seq in community pipelines (e.g., Currently, MACS2 is the default peak caller of the ENCODE ATAC-seq pipeline. from Yan et al., Genome Biology, 2020, https://doi.org/10.1186/s13059-020-1929-3). Since the dataset analysed here is ATAC-based, using MACS2 is both appropriate and consistent with community standards.
We acknowledge your point regarding the potential methodological bias and have added a clarification in the revised manuscript (Lines 179–183) to explicitly discuss this limitation and the rationale behind our tool selection.
Reviewer #2’s additional comments to cover Reviewer #1
Comment 2-4. Response to comment 2 by Reviewer #1
The authors have improved the text, but their response still lacks clarity on the rule of thumb or decision criterion for classifying DNA sequence patterns into cPeak vs. non-cPeak. It would strengthen the manuscript if they could provide more details on the exact procedure.
Response:
Thank you for the suggestion. We have now clarified the decision criterion for distinguishing cPeaks from non-cPeaks. Specifically, we added a new subsection titled “Determination of threshold for predicting additional cPeaks” (Lines 781–787), where we describe how the threshold was derived from the masking experiments. In brief, we examined the predicted score distributions of masked cell type- or tissue-specific cPeaks, identified an elbow point (the value at which the frequency of scores began to rise sharply) in each case, and averaged these values across all datasets to obtain a unified threshold of 0.872. This empirically derived threshold was then used to classify additional predicted cPeaks.
Comment 2-5. Response to comment 3 by Reviewer #1
The reviewer 1 raised a key concern: if the training dataset used to generate cPeaks does not include one cell type (e.g., a rare cell type), what is the rationale for expecting cPeaks to aid in the discovery of that cell type? The authors’ current response does not sufficiently address this. Intuitively, if the training data lacks signals from a particular cell type, then simply using the aggregated cPeak list would not necessarily enable its detection. The authors should provide a stronger explanation or empirical demonstration of why and how cPeaks could facilitate rare cell type identification under such conditions.
Response:
Thank you for the opportunity to clarify our rationale regarding rare cell types. We would like to clarity that the advantage of cPeaks lies in two aspects.
First, cPeaks address the limitation of conventional pseudo-bulk peak calling, which is strongly biased toward prevalent signals. Accessibility sites from rare populations are often treated as noise and filtered out during peak calling, meaning that the information is lost before downstream analysis. In contrast, cPeaks are constructed across a wide range of tissues and cell types, independent of their abundance in any single dataset. This avoids prevalence-driven filtering and ensures that many informative regions relevant to rare populations remain in the reference feature space.
Second, to further address the scenario where a cell type or tissue is entirely absent from the training data, we use a CNN to predict additional cPeaks. As shown in Fig. 2c, the model achieved a mean AUC of 91.67% when predicting peaks specific to cell types or tissues that were masked during training. This demonstrates that even for unseen populations, most of their accessible regions can still be recovered as predicted cPeaks. Together, the broad construction of cPeaks and the predictive capacity of the CNN ensure that rare or missing cell types are not excluded from analysis. We have added further clarification on this point in Lines 427–432.

Responses to Reviewer #5’s comments
General response to Reviewer #5
We sincerely thank you for carefully reviewing our manuscript and for also taking the extra step of examining how we addressed the comments from the previous reviewer. Your feedback helped us substantially improve both the clarity and the rigor of the manuscript. Following your suggestions, we revised the text, clarified details, and added new analyses. Our detailed, point-by-point responses are provided below.
Comment 3-3 (presentation order of similarity analysis)
General comment: You added cPeak-level shape-consistency results (Fig. R12), which is excellent, but the paragraph order was not reversed as originally suggested. While this is a stylistic matter, switching the intermediate- vs final-peak sections would make the logic flow more intuitive for readers.
Detailed comment: Although the authors kept the original paragraph order (justifying the merging strategy with intermediate-peak results before introducing the new cPeak analysis), the added Fig. R12 and Suppl. S1e-f now demonstrate robust similarity for the final cPeaks, the scientific concern is resolved even if the stylistic request to swap those sections is unmet.
Response:
Thank you for the suggestion. We fully agree that readers are primarily interested in the final cPeaks. At the same time, we believe that showing the stability of the intermediate peaks is essential to justify the feasibility of constructing consensus peaks, which is a central part of our argument.
To better balance these two aspects, we have made two changes in the revision. First, we shortened the intermediate-peak section so that the key message is easier to grasp (Lines 110–135). Second, we moved the intermediate-peak results to the Supplementary Information (now Fig. S1c–d) and highlighted the final cPeak results in the main text (now Fig. 1d). We appreciate that this is largely a stylistic matter, and we hope that the current restructuring strikes a good balance between logical justification and readability.
Comment 3-4 (TF-binding footprints in Fig. 1c/f)
General comment: No footprinting analysis was added; the manuscript now only states that read-level data were unavailable. Even a limited demonstration (e.g., aggregate cut-site metaplots for one representative ENCODE BAM) would provide direct evidence of TF occupancy and fully satisfy the request.
Detailed comment: The authors states that transcription-factor footprinting requires base-resolution read coverage, which they did not retain when summarising peaks; they therefore offer no new analyses or figure updates and only suggest footprinting for “future work.” A review of the revised manuscript confirms that no footprinting results (or TF-binding evidence) were added anywhere, so the original request remains unmet.
At minimum, the authors could have downloaded one high-depth ENCODE bulk ATAC-seq BAM that matches your example peaks, extracted single-base Tn5 cut sites, scanned those peaks for frequent JASPAR motifs (e.g., CTCF or AP-1), and produced an aggregate ±50 bp metaplot showing the expected central dip flanked by higher insertion density; a simple footprint-depth statistic and one or two IGV snapshots would have provided direct, base-resolution evidence of TF occupancy without re-processing all 624 samples.
Response:
Thank you. Following your advice, we performed an additional demonstration using publicly available read-level ATAC-seq data to directly visualize transcription factor (TF) footprints. Specifically, we downloaded the original bulk ATAC-seq BAM files from a classical study (Buenrostro et al., Nature Methods, 2013, https://doi.org/10.1038/nmeth.2688). To ensure computational efficiency, we focused our analysis on chromosome 4. Using the TOBIAS framework, we conducted TF-footprinting analysis within the open chromatin regions defined by cPeaks.
We obtained clear footprinting patterns and visualized the aggregated ATAC-seq cut-site profiles and heatmaps. Representative examples for the canonical motifs CTCF and BATF are shown, both displaying the expected central depletion of insertions flanked by regions of increased cut-site density, consistent with characteristic TF occupancy signatures (Figure R 3).
These results demonstrate that regions defined by cPeaks indeed cover TF-binding sites and that the cPeak framework can support footprint-based analyses when base-resolution data are available. Thank you again for your valuable suggestion.
Figure R 3 Footprinting of CTCF (left) and BATF (right) motifs within the open chromatin regions defined by cPeaks.
Comment 3-6 (PBMC benchmark)
General comment: The additional PBMC-10k dataset and QC filters are welcome, but two gaps remain:
(i) Scalability to a truly large PBMC collection (≥ 50 k cells) is still untested.
(ii) A dedicated doublet-detection tool (e.g., Scrublet, DoubletFinder) has not been applied. Including one run and reporting the percentage of flagged cells would strengthen confidence in the benchmark.
Detailed comment: The benchmarking section is substantially improved—additional feature sets, clearer clustering metrics, UMAP examples, and a second PBMC dataset now appear. However, the new PBMC-10k still falls short of the very large cell counts suggested, and doublet handling remains minimal. Thus Comment 3-6 is largely but not completely resolved.
To finish closing the gap you should still (i) benchmark on a genuinely large PBMC dataset—one of the public 50 k–100 k cell collections—so that scalability to tens-of-thousands of cells is demonstrated, (ii) apply a dedicated doublet-detection tool such as Scrublet, DoubletFinder or AMULET and report how many cells are removed and whether results change, and (iii optional) include at least one TEA-seq or other multimodal dataset (or an unsupervised variant of the united-peaks reference) to round out the cross-platform comparison.
Response:
(i) Benchmarking on a larger-scale dataset
Thank you for highlighting the importance of testing scalability. In response, we downloaded the paired scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq dataset GSE190992. After quality control and doublet removal using the ArchR doublet-detection module, we obtained 48,487 high-confidence scATAC-seq cells for downstream analysis, which we refer to as PBMC-48k. Benchmarking results (Figure R 4) showed that cPeaks perform comparably or better in detecting rare cell types at this scale, supporting their robustness in large datasets. These results have been added to Fig. S5e–h and described in Lines 459–463 and 977–983 of the revised manuscript.
Figure R 4 Rare cell type discovery using cPeaks on the PBMC-48k dataset. (e) The proportion of each cell type in the PBMC-48k dataset. Three rare cell types were less than 1% (the dashed black line): cDC2, Eryth, and B intermediate. (f) The UMAP plots of the PBMC-48k dataset analyzed by each reference set. Each dot represented one cell. Different colors represented different clusters. (g) Performance of clustering accuracy using different reference peak sets in the PBMC-48k dataset. (h) The Venn plot of the number of differential accessible regions calculated by cPeaks and other reference sets for pDCs in the PBMC-48k dataset.
(ii) Doublet-detection tool
Specifically, we processed the scATAC-seq data using the ArchR pipeline, identified 9.08% of cells as doublets with the addDoubletScores function, and removed them using filterDoublets. To further evaluate the impact of doublet removal, we also performed the same analysis without filtering doublets and found that cPeaks no longer achieved the best clustering performance (Figure R 5). This indicates that cPeaks perform particularly well on high-quality datasets with proper doublet removal. Details of doublet removal have been added in Lines 978–979.
In addition, we confirmed that all datasets analyzed in the original manuscript had already undergone doublet filtering by their original authors, so the results presented previously were not affected by doublet contamination.
Figure R 5 Performance of clustering accuracy using different reference peak sets on the PBMC-48k dataset without doublet removal.
(iii) Benchmarking on TEA-seq
Regarding TEA-seq, we explored available datasets (e.g., https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.63632) but were unable to obtain reliable cell type labels from the original data to support a meaningful benchmark. We also contacted the corresponding authors for clarification but did not receive a response. In addition, our attempts to reproduce their published analysis pipeline did not yield results consistent with those reported in the article. For these reasons, we were unable to include a TEA-seq benchmark in the current revision.
Comment 3-8 (pseudotime analysis with alternative feature sets)
General Comment: The new lineage-wise plots using cPeaks clarify the trend, yet the analysis is still shown for cPeaks alone. Please add the same pseudotime/UMAP plots for at least one other reference (e.g., CATLAS cCREs) or provide quantitative evidence that those references cannot support an equivalent well-positioned-peak metric.
Detailed Comment: The presentation is clearer and the new pseudotime plots meet requests (b) and (c). However, point (a) remains only partially resolved: the manuscript still lacks a side-by-side pseudotime/UMAP demonstration with at least one other reference set, so the claimed uniqueness of the well-positioned-cPeak metric is asserted rather than shown.
(a) is still incomplete: to substantiate the claimed novelty, please include the same pseudotime/UMAP analysis with at least one alternative reference (e.g., CATLAS cCREs or cDHSs) or provide quantitative evidence that those feature sets cannot support an equivalent well-positioned-peak metric.
Response:
Thank you for this suggestion. We would like to emphasize that the well-positioned-cPeak metric is a property unique to cPeaks and cannot be directly derived from other reference sets. Our goal in this section was not to argue that only cPeaks can recover developmental trajectories, but to demonstrate the distinctive biological insights enabled by this metric.
In line with your comment, we repeated the pseudotime/UMAP analysis using CATLAS cCREs and cDHSs (Figure R 6). The overall trajectories were similar across reference sets; however, only cPeaks and cCREs revealed the two sub-branches within the RGC lineage that were noted in the original study (Figure R 7), whereas cDHSs failed to capture this structure. Since the original work did not provide detailed analysis of these sub-branches, we cannot ascertain their biological significance at this stage.
To avoid overstating the claims, we have revised the text to make clear that this analysis is intended to highlight the unique role of the well-positioned-cPeak metric in developmental studies, rather than to suggest exclusive superiority of cPeaks in trajectory reconstruction (Lines 523-524, 530-531).
Figure R 6 UMAP visualization of the 8-week retina scATAC-seq data analyzed by different reference sets, colored by cell types (top) and pseudotime (bottom).
Figure R 7 UMAP visualization of the 8-week retina scATAC-seq data from the original paper (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.celrep.2021.110294). Cells are colored by cell types (left), pseudotime (right).
Comment 3-17 (minor) (annotation method)
General Comment: The revision retains the Seurat/Signac anchor strategy without testing any newer scATAC annotation tools. Running a contemporary method such as ArchR label transfer, scGLUE or CellTypist—and showing that conclusions remain unchanged—would address the original concern.
Detailed Comment: I appreciate the justification for retaining the Seurat/Signac anchor approach, but because no alternative annotation method was tested the limitation highlighted in Comment 3-17 persists; incorporating at least one contemporary scATAC-labelling tool (e.g., ArchR label transfer or scGLUE) would strengthen confidence in the annotation robustness.
Response:
Thank you. As part of the new PBMC-48k analysis described in our response to Comment 3-6, we applied ArchR’s label transfer approach to annotate scATAC-seq cells. Specifically, for the scRNA-seq data, cells with predicted.celltype.l2.score > 0.9 were retained as high-confidence annotations. These cells were then used to transfer labels to scATAC-seq data via the addGeneIntegrationMatrix function in ArchR, which also provides a predictedScore for each assigned label. We selected 45,761 scATAC-seq cells with a predictedScore > 0.9 for downstream analyses.
As shown in Figure R 4, the results were consistent with PBMC-8k which transferred labels with Seurat, thereby confirming that our conclusions are robust to the choice of annotation method. We have added the details of label transferring in Lines 977-983.
Comment 3-19c (minor) (comparability of UMAP projections)
General Comment: UMAPs are still calculated separately for each dataset, limiting direct visual comparison across life stages. A joint embedding (or at least side-by-side UMAPs generated with the same global coordinates) would make cross-dataset patterns easier to interpret.
Detailed Comment: Points (a) and (b) are fully satisfied. Point (c) is only partially resolved because the figures still rely on distinct projections, limiting direct visual comparison across datasets.
The added GO-term heatmap reference and the new life-stage-coloured UMAPs clarify the biology nicely; however, because each dataset is still visualised with its own UMAP embedding, cross-dataset comparisons remain difficult. A joint projection (or at least side-by-side UMAPs created with identical global coordinates) would fully resolve the comparability issue noted in Comment 3-19.
Response:
Thank you for the suggestion. We have now performed a joint embedding by visualizing the different developmental stages of the retina together (Figure R 8), and the results have been added to Fig. S7a, S7d, and Lines 519, 537. Consistent with our previous observations, the well-positioned-cPeak ratio shows an overall decrease with developmental progression, supporting the biological trend described in the main text.
Figure R 8 (a) The UMAP plot of all scATAC-seq data collected from retina. Cells are colored by sample labels (left) and cell types (right). (d) The UMAP plot of all scATAC-seq data collected from retina. Cells are colored by well-positioned-cPeak ratios.
Remarks on code availability
I did not run it, but looked at whether the repo was usable.
The repository is usable and largely reproducible for downstream analyses (mapping fragments, rerunning benchmarks). Re-generating the entire resource (merging 624 datasets or replicating the CNN training) would still require substantial external data and compute, but that is typical for large genomics references.
Suggested very minor improvements:
(i) Add a requirements.txt or environment.yml with tested versions.
(ii) Upload the pre-trained CNN weights (or provide an S3/Zenodo link) and a small test fragment file for a quick end-to-end smoke test.
(iii) Include a minimal CI job that runs map2cpeak on the toy dataset to ensure code health over time.
(iv) With these tweaks, the repo would be an even more robust community resource.
Response:
Thank you for these practical suggestions. We have made the following updates:
(i) added a requirements.txt file specifying tested versions at https://github.com/MengQiuchen/cPeaks/blob/main/deepCNN/requirements.txt and https://github.com/MengQiuchen/cPeaks/blob/main/requirements.txt;
(ii) uploaded the pre-trained CNN weights at:
https://github.com/MengQiuchen/cPeaks/tree/main/deepCNN/save_model;
(iii) provided a small test fragment file for running a quick map2cpeak end-to-end test at:
https://github.com/MengQiuchen/cPeaks/tree/main/map2cpeak/demo, and implemented a minimal CI job at https://github.com/MengQiuchen/cPeaks/blob/main/.github/workflows/smoke-test.yml.
We hope that these improvements can make the repository more robust and user-friendly for the community.
Responses to Reviewer #2’s comments
The authors have addressed most of our comments. One minor issue remains: Reviewer 1’s question concerns unobserved cell types—i.e., cases with zero abundance in the training data. In that setting, how can cPeaks serve as a valid peak list for that cell type? The hold-out (masked) evaluation in Fig. 2c helps address this and should be emphasized. However, the newly added sentence “cPeaks are constructed across a wide range of tissues and cell types, independent of their prevalence in any single dataset…” is misleading. “Independent” is ambiguous and overstates the claim. We understand the intent is to say that aggregating across datasets reduces prevalence-driven filtering (so rare-accessible loci are less likely to be lost), not that cPeaks are statistically independent of training composition.
Reponses:
Thank you for the helpful feedback. We agree with your point regarding the ambiguity of the term “independent.” We have revised the sentence in Line 429 to read: “cPeaks are constructed across a wide range of tissues and cell types, and their composition is not dominated by the prevalence of any single dataset.” This change more accurately reflects our intended meaning.
Responses to Reviewer #5’s comments
All six points are addressed to a standard I would consider acceptable for a second-round review. I’d like to thank the authors for addressing these comments.
The last tweak I would still ask for before acceptance, is to move some figures in the rebuttal into the Supplement. It would greatly benefit the manuscript in my opinion.
For instance you could migrate rebuttal Figs. R3, R5, and R6–R7 into the Supplement (either as new Supplementary Figs, or as additional panels) so that the footprinting evidence, the no-doublet control, and the alternative-feature pseudotime comparisons are part of the archived record.
Reponses:
Thank you very much for your suggestions. We have incorporated your recommendations as follows:
l We have added Fig. R3 to the manuscript as Fig. S2c, cited it in Lines 299–230, and included an explanation of the footprinting experiment in Lines 830–834.
l We have added Fig. R5 as Fig. S5i, cited it, and discussed the results in Lines 989–991.
l We have added Fig. R6 as Fig. S7d, and cited it in Line 531.
l We did not include Fig. R7, as it corresponds to figures from the original manuscript (Ref. [34] in our paper). However, we added a note in Line 528 indicating that the trajectories are “similar to the trend reported in the original study,” to help readers better interpret the results.
