(c) Considering the existence of doublets
In our study, we followed quality control procedures to minimize their impact. Specifically, we excluded cells with an abnormally high total number of fragments, which are commonly indicative of doublets. This filtering step was applied prior to downstream analysis to reduce the presence of technical artifacts. Although we did not use a dedicated doublet detection algorithm, the resulting clusters showed clear separation and consistent label transfer from scRNA-seq, suggesting that any remaining doublets did not substantially affect our results. We have now added a clarification of this filtering criterion in the revised Methods section (Line 928).

We consider “rare” to refer to cell types that appear at low proportions within a given sequencing dataset. This definition may not correspond to biological rarity. The sampling bias or technical limitations in sequencing may also result in lower capture rates for certain cell types. The limited representation of these “rare” cells poses challenges for downstream analysis. For example, in the PBMC-8k dataset used in our analysis, pDC cells accounts for less than 2% of the total cells, and they cannot be well separated by genomic bins as reference, as shown in the new Fig. S4b. According to our definition, these cells fall within the category of rare cell types that are the focus of our analysis.
In the revised version, we retain the use of “rare” for consistency with common usage in the field but added explanation to more precisely define our intent (Line 427 and 487-489).

The purpose of evaluating the model on held-out, tissue- or cell-type-specific cPeaks was not to assign predicted peaks to specific tissues, but rather to test the model’s generalizability: whether it can recover potentially accessible regions that were not present in the training data. These regions, though observed in particular tissues, are treated in our analysis as sequence-defined elements whose accessibility may depend on cellular context.

Importantly, our downstream analysis centers on plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDCs), a well-defined population with distinct clustering and marker profiles. As such, we believe the annotation method used does not materially affect our conclusions.

Responses to Reviewer #2’s comments
General response to Reviewer #2
We sincerely thank you for your careful and constructive feedback, and especially for taking the additional effort to review our responses to Reviewer #1. We greatly appreciate the time and thought you invested in helping us strengthen the manuscript. Following your suggestions, we have substantially revised the text, clarified methodological details, and added new analyses where appropriate. Our detailed, point-by-point responses are provided below.
Comment 2-1. Clarification of Figure 1d and Peak Shape Similarity Analysis
The revised Figure 1d helps clarify the use of MACS2 and the overall strategy for generating cPeaks. I recommend that the authors provide additional detail on how the Pearson correlation was calculated. It would also be helpful to define the two negative control groups and the true peak group more clearly. Furthermore, I suggest avoiding the term “true peaks” when referring to the experimental group, since these peaks are still based on estimates from observed ATAC-seq or DNase-seq data and not experimentally validated ground truth.
Response:
Thank you for the helpful suggestions. To improve clarity, we have substantially revised the description of the peak shape similarity analysis in the Methods (lines 700–711). In the revised text, we describe how the genomic window was defined, how peaks were trimmed or zero-padded for alignment, and how base-pair-level values were used to calculate the PCC. We also provide clearer definitions of the two control groups. To further aid understanding, we added a new schematic (Figure R 1, or Fig. S1b in the revised manuscript) that illustrates the calculation procedure and the construction of the two control groups.
In addition, we replaced the term “true peak pairs” with “paired peaks” throughout the manuscript to avoid implying experimentally validated ground truth. We believe these revisions address your concerns and make the analysis more transparent and rigorous.
Figure R 1 Diagram of PCC computation and control group definitions.
Comment 2-2. Concern Regarding Potential Model Circularity
The authors appear to have misunderstood the original question regarding circularity. The concern is whether the current training process, which uses DNA sequence and cPeaks derived from observed ATAC-seq data, might predict novel peaks that are not included in the existing cPeak list. If those novel peaks were then added to the cPeak list and used to retrain the model, it is unclear whether this would result in further predictions of additional peaks. This raises the possibility of an iterative feedback process without a clear stopping criterion. The authors are encouraged to clarify whether such retraining was considered and whether this approach would be methodologically appropriate.
Response:
Thank you for further clarifying this question. Indeed, iteratively expanding the training set with model-predicted positives is a potential strategy explored in other contexts, such as positive-unlabeled (PU) learning. Following your suggestion, we evaluated whether such an iterative retraining approach could improve our model. Specifically, we added all predicted cPeaks (~0.28 million) to the training set and retrained the CNN. The updated model subsequently predicted an additional ~0.22 million peaks with scores above the threshold. Repeating this procedure led to the identification of progressively more peaks until nearly all candidate regions were classified as cPeaks, indicating uncontrolled expansion of predictions (Figure R 2). The results suggested a clear behavioral drift in the retrained model: with each iteration, the CNN increasingly classified nearly all candidate regions as positive. We hypothesize that this is likely due to the fixed-window prediction scheme used by the CNN, which does not provide precise peak boundary information. These results indicate that iterative retraining may propagate boundary noise and accumulate errors rather than improve model performance. Therefore, we consider the one-time training strategy adopted in this study to be the most appropriate and stable approach.
To help readers better understand this point, we have added a brief explanation in the revised manuscript (Lines 656–657, 803–805), noting that improving the prediction procedure to more accurately capture peak boundaries will be an important direction for future work.
Figure R 2 Number of newly/accumulated predicted cPeaks identified after each iteration of model retraining.
Comment 2-3. Benchmarking Comparison in Figure 1h
The comparison in Figure 1h may be affected by differences in the peak-calling tools used. Both cPeaks and CATLAS cCREs were generated using MACS2, but cDHSs were generated using Hotspot2. This makes it hard to tell whether the performance differences are due to biological signals or the choice of tool. Please clarify this point in the manuscript and consider discussing how tool differences may affect the results.
Response:
Thank you for the suggestion. We agree that the comparison in Figure 1h could potentially be influenced by differences in peak-calling algorithms, as cDHSs were originally generated with Hotspot2, whereas both cPeaks and CATLAS cCREs were produced using MACS2.
To directly address this concern, we attempted to reanalyse the data using Hotspot2 and perform comparison. However, despite our extensive technical efforts (including reimplementation of preprocessing scripts, setting computational environments on different servers, optimization of input data, and multiple recovery strategies), the analysis could not be completed successfully due to a fatal data-dependent bug in the core hotspot2_part1 module. This issue, which causes silent crashes even on validated datasets, reflects the fact that Hotspot2 has not been actively maintained for nearly a decade and is no longer compatible with nowadays computing environments.
We therefore approached the question conceptually. MACS2 is now commonly adopted as the default peak-calling tool for ATAC-seq in community pipelines (e.g., Currently, MACS2 is the default peak caller of the ENCODE ATAC-seq pipeline. from Yan et al., Genome Biology, 2020, https://doi.org/10.1186/s13059-020-1929-3). Since the dataset analysed here is ATAC-based, using MACS2 is both appropriate and consistent with community standards.
We acknowledge your point regarding the potential methodological bias and have added a clarification in the revised manuscript (Lines 179–183) to explicitly discuss this limitation and the rationale behind our tool selection.
Reviewer #2’s additional comments to cover Reviewer #1
Comment 2-4. Response to comment 2 by Reviewer #1
The authors have improved the text, but their response still lacks clarity on the rule of thumb or decision criterion for classifying DNA sequence patterns into cPeak vs. non-cPeak. It would strengthen the manuscript if they could provide more details on the exact procedure.
Response:
Thank you for the suggestion. We have now clarified the decision criterion for distinguishing cPeaks from non-cPeaks. Specifically, we added a new subsection titled “Determination of threshold for predicting additional cPeaks” (Lines 781–787), where we describe how the threshold was derived from the masking experiments. In brief, we examined the predicted score distributions of masked cell type- or tissue-specific cPeaks, identified an elbow point (the value at which the frequency of scores began to rise sharply) in each case, and averaged these values across all datasets to obtain a unified threshold of 0.872. This empirically derived threshold was then used to classify additional predicted cPeaks.
Comment 2-5. Response to comment 3 by Reviewer #1
The reviewer 1 raised a key concern: if the training dataset used to generate cPeaks does not include one cell type (e.g., a rare cell type), what is the rationale for expecting cPeaks to aid in the discovery of that cell type? The authors’ current response does not sufficiently address this. Intuitively, if the training data lacks signals from a particular cell type, then simply using the aggregated cPeak list would not necessarily enable its detection. The authors should provide a stronger explanation or empirical demonstration of why and how cPeaks could facilitate rare cell type identification under such conditions.
Response:
Thank you for the opportunity to clarify our rationale regarding rare cell types. We would like to clarity that the advantage of cPeaks lies in two aspects.
First, cPeaks address the limitation of conventional pseudo-bulk peak calling, which is strongly biased toward prevalent signals. Accessibility sites from rare populations are often treated as noise and filtered out during peak calling, meaning that the information is lost before downstream analysis. In contrast, cPeaks are constructed across a wide range of tissues and cell types, independent of their abundance in any single dataset. This avoids prevalence-driven filtering and ensures that many informative regions relevant to rare populations remain in the reference feature space.
Second, to further address the scenario where a cell type or tissue is entirely absent from the training data, we use a CNN to predict additional cPeaks. As shown in Fig. 2c, the model achieved a mean AUC of 91.67% when predicting peaks specific to cell types or tissues that were masked during training. This demonstrates that even for unseen populations, most of their accessible regions can still be recovered as predicted cPeaks. Together, the broad construction of cPeaks and the predictive capacity of the CNN ensure that rare or missing cell types are not excluded from analysis. We have added further clarification on this point in Lines 427–432.

Responses to Reviewer #5’s comments
General response to Reviewer #5
We sincerely thank you for carefully reviewing our manuscript and for also taking the extra step of examining how we addressed the comments from the previous reviewer. Your feedback helped us substantially improve both the clarity and the rigor of the manuscript. Following your suggestions, we revised the text, clarified details, and added new analyses. Our detailed, point-by-point responses are provided below.
Comment 3-3 (presentation order of similarity analysis)
General comment: You added cPeak-level shape-consistency results (Fig. R12), which is excellent, but the paragraph order was not reversed as originally suggested. While this is a stylistic matter, switching the intermediate- vs final-peak sections would make the logic flow more intuitive for readers.
Detailed comment: Although the authors kept the original paragraph order (justifying the merging strategy with intermediate-peak results before introducing the new cPeak analysis), the added Fig. R12 and Suppl. S1e-f now demonstrate robust similarity for the final cPeaks, the scientific concern is resolved even if the stylistic request to swap those sections is unmet.
Response:
Thank you for the suggestion. We fully agree that readers are primarily interested in the final cPeaks. At the same time, we believe that showing the stability of the intermediate peaks is essential to justify the feasibility of constructing consensus peaks, which is a central part of our argument.
To better balance these two aspects, we have made two changes in the revision. First, we shortened the intermediate-peak section so that the key message is easier to grasp (Lines 110–135). Second, we moved the intermediate-peak results to the Supplementary Information (now Fig. S1c–d) and highlighted the final cPeak results in the main text (now Fig. 1d). We appreciate that this is largely a stylistic matter, and we hope that the current restructuring strikes a good balance between logical justification and readability.
Comment 3-4 (TF-binding footprints in Fig. 1c/f)
General comment: No footprinting analysis was added; the manuscript now only states that read-level data were unavailable. Even a limited demonstration (e.g., aggregate cut-site metaplots for one representative ENCODE BAM) would provide direct evidence of TF occupancy and fully satisfy the request.
Detailed comment: The authors states that transcription-factor footprinting requires base-resolution read coverage, which they did not retain when summarising peaks; they therefore offer no new analyses or figure updates and only suggest footprinting for “future work.” A review of the revised manuscript confirms that no footprinting results (or TF-binding evidence) were added anywhere, so the original request remains unmet.
At minimum, the authors could have downloaded one high-depth ENCODE bulk ATAC-seq BAM that matches your example peaks, extracted single-base Tn5 cut sites, scanned those peaks for frequent JASPAR motifs (e.g., CTCF or AP-1), and produced an aggregate ±50 bp metaplot showing the expected central dip flanked by higher insertion density; a simple footprint-depth statistic and one or two IGV snapshots would have provided direct, base-resolution evidence of TF occupancy without re-processing all 624 samples.
Response:
Thank you. Following your advice, we performed an additional demonstration using publicly available read-level ATAC-seq data to directly visualize transcription factor (TF) footprints. Specifically, we downloaded the original bulk ATAC-seq BAM files from a classical study (Buenrostro et al., Nature Methods, 2013, https://doi.org/10.1038/nmeth.2688). To ensure computational efficiency, we focused our analysis on chromosome 4. Using the TOBIAS framework, we conducted TF-footprinting analysis within the open chromatin regions defined by cPeaks.
We obtained clear footprinting patterns and visualized the aggregated ATAC-seq cut-site profiles and heatmaps. Representative examples for the canonical motifs CTCF and BATF are shown, both displaying the expected central depletion of insertions flanked by regions of increased cut-site density, consistent with characteristic TF occupancy signatures (Figure R 3).
These results demonstrate that regions defined by cPeaks indeed cover TF-binding sites and that the cPeak framework can support footprint-based analyses when base-resolution data are available. Thank you again for your valuable suggestion.
Figure R 3 Footprinting of CTCF (left) and BATF (right) motifs within the open chromatin regions defined by cPeaks.
Comment 3-6 (PBMC benchmark)
General comment: The additional PBMC-10k dataset and QC filters are welcome, but two gaps remain:
(i) Scalability to a truly large PBMC collection (≥ 50 k cells) is still untested.
(ii) A dedicated doublet-detection tool (e.g., Scrublet, DoubletFinder) has not been applied. Including one run and reporting the percentage of flagged cells would strengthen confidence in the benchmark.
Detailed comment: The benchmarking section is substantially improved—additional feature sets, clearer clustering metrics, UMAP examples, and a second PBMC dataset now appear. However, the new PBMC-10k still falls short of the very large cell counts suggested, and doublet handling remains minimal. Thus Comment 3-6 is largely but not completely resolved.
To finish closing the gap you should still (i) benchmark on a genuinely large PBMC dataset—one of the public 50 k–100 k cell collections—so that scalability to tens-of-thousands of cells is demonstrated, (ii) apply a dedicated doublet-detection tool such as Scrublet, DoubletFinder or AMULET and report how many cells are removed and whether results change, and (iii optional) include at least one TEA-seq or other multimodal dataset (or an unsupervised variant of the united-peaks reference) to round out the cross-platform comparison.
Response:
(i) Benchmarking on a larger-scale dataset
Thank you for highlighting the importance of testing scalability. In response, we downloaded the paired scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq dataset GSE190992. After quality control and doublet removal using the ArchR doublet-detection module, we obtained 48,487 high-confidence scATAC-seq cells for downstream analysis, which we refer to as PBMC-48k. Benchmarking results (Figure R 4) showed that cPeaks perform comparably or better in detecting rare cell types at this scale, supporting their robustness in large datasets. These results have been added to Fig. S5e–h and described in Lines 459–463 and 977–983 of the revised manuscript.
Figure R 4 Rare cell type discovery using cPeaks on the PBMC-48k dataset. (e) The proportion of each cell type in the PBMC-48k dataset. Three rare cell types were less than 1% (the dashed black line): cDC2, Eryth, and B intermediate. (f) The UMAP plots of the PBMC-48k dataset analyzed by each reference set. Each dot represented one cell. Different colors represented different clusters. (g) Performance of clustering accuracy using different reference peak sets in the PBMC-48k dataset. (h) The Venn plot of the number of differential accessible regions calculated by cPeaks and other reference sets for pDCs in the PBMC-48k dataset.
(ii) Doublet-detection tool
Specifically, we processed the scATAC-seq data using the ArchR pipeline, identified 9.08% of cells as doublets with the addDoubletScores function, and removed them using filterDoublets. To further evaluate the impact of doublet removal, we also performed the same analysis without filtering doublets and found that cPeaks no longer achieved the best clustering performance (Figure R 5). This indicates that cPeaks perform particularly well on high-quality datasets with proper doublet removal. Details of doublet removal have been added in Lines 978–979.
In addition, we confirmed that all datasets analyzed in the original manuscript had already undergone doublet filtering by their original authors, so the results presented previously were not affected by doublet contamination.
Figure R 5 Performance of clustering accuracy using different reference peak sets on the PBMC-48k dataset without doublet removal.
(iii) Benchmarking on TEA-seq
Regarding TEA-seq, we explored available datasets (e.g., https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.63632) but were unable to obtain reliable cell type labels from the original data to support a meaningful benchmark. We also contacted the corresponding authors for clarification but did not receive a response. In addition, our attempts to reproduce their published analysis pipeline did not yield results consistent with those reported in the article. For these reasons, we were unable to include a TEA-seq benchmark in the current revision.
Comment 3-8 (pseudotime analysis with alternative feature sets)
General Comment: The new lineage-wise plots using cPeaks clarify the trend, yet the analysis is still shown for cPeaks alone. Please add the same pseudotime/UMAP plots for at least one other reference (e.g., CATLAS cCREs) or provide quantitative evidence that those references cannot support an equivalent well-positioned-peak metric.
Detailed Comment: The presentation is clearer and the new pseudotime plots meet requests (b) and (c). However, point (a) remains only partially resolved: the manuscript still lacks a side-by-side pseudotime/UMAP demonstration with at least one other reference set, so the claimed uniqueness of the well-positioned-cPeak metric is asserted rather than shown.
(a) is still incomplete: to substantiate the claimed novelty, please include the same pseudotime/UMAP analysis with at least one alternative reference (e.g., CATLAS cCREs or cDHSs) or provide quantitative evidence that those feature sets cannot support an equivalent well-positioned-peak metric.
Response:
Thank you for this suggestion. We would like to emphasize that the well-positioned-cPeak metric is a property unique to cPeaks and cannot be directly derived from other reference sets. Our goal in this section was not to argue that only cPeaks can recover developmental trajectories, but to demonstrate the distinctive biological insights enabled by this metric.
In line with your comment, we repeated the pseudotime/UMAP analysis using CATLAS cCREs and cDHSs (Figure R 6). The overall trajectories were similar across reference sets; however, only cPeaks and cCREs revealed the two sub-branches within the RGC lineage that were noted in the original study (Figure R 7), whereas cDHSs failed to capture this structure. Since the original work did not provide detailed analysis of these sub-branches, we cannot ascertain their biological significance at this stage.
To avoid overstating the claims, we have revised the text to make clear that this analysis is intended to highlight the unique role of the well-positioned-cPeak metric in developmental studies, rather than to suggest exclusive superiority of cPeaks in trajectory reconstruction (Lines 523-524, 530-531).
Figure R 6 UMAP visualization of the 8-week retina scATAC-seq data analyzed by different reference sets, colored by cell types (top) and pseudotime (bottom).
Figure R 7 UMAP visualization of the 8-week retina scATAC-seq data from the original paper (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.celrep.2021.110294). Cells are colored by cell types (left), pseudotime (right).
Comment 3-17 (minor) (annotation method)
General Comment: The revision retains the Seurat/Signac anchor strategy without testing any newer scATAC annotation tools. Running a contemporary method such as ArchR label transfer, scGLUE or CellTypist—and showing that conclusions remain unchanged—would address the original concern.
Detailed Comment: I appreciate the justification for retaining the Seurat/Signac anchor approach, but because no alternative annotation method was tested the limitation highlighted in Comment 3-17 persists; incorporating at least one contemporary scATAC-labelling tool (e.g., ArchR label transfer or scGLUE) would strengthen confidence in the annotation robustness.
Response:
Thank you. As part of the new PBMC-48k analysis described in our response to Comment 3-6, we applied ArchR’s label transfer approach to annotate scATAC-seq cells. Specifically, for the scRNA-seq data, cells with predicted.celltype.l2.score > 0.9 were retained as high-confidence annotations. These cells were then used to transfer labels to scATAC-seq data via the addGeneIntegrationMatrix function in ArchR, which also provides a predictedScore for each assigned label. We selected 45,761 scATAC-seq cells with a predictedScore > 0.9 for downstream analyses.
As shown in Figure R 4, the results were consistent with PBMC-8k which transferred labels with Seurat, thereby confirming that our conclusions are robust to the choice of annotation method. We have added the details of label transferring in Lines 977-983.
Comment 3-19c (minor) (comparability of UMAP projections)
General Comment: UMAPs are still calculated separately for each dataset, limiting direct visual comparison across life stages. A joint embedding (or at least side-by-side UMAPs generated with the same global coordinates) would make cross-dataset patterns easier to interpret.
Detailed Comment: Points (a) and (b) are fully satisfied. Point (c) is only partially resolved because the figures still rely on distinct projections, limiting direct visual comparison across datasets.
The added GO-term heatmap reference and the new life-stage-coloured UMAPs clarify the biology nicely; however, because each dataset is still visualised with its own UMAP embedding, cross-dataset comparisons remain difficult. A joint projection (or at least side-by-side UMAPs created with identical global coordinates) would fully resolve the comparability issue noted in Comment 3-19.
Response:
Thank you for the suggestion. We have now performed a joint embedding by visualizing the different developmental stages of the retina together (Figure R 8), and the results have been added to Fig. S7a, S7d, and Lines 519, 537. Consistent with our previous observations, the well-positioned-cPeak ratio shows an overall decrease with developmental progression, supporting the biological trend described in the main text.
Figure R 8 (a) The UMAP plot of all scATAC-seq data collected from retina. Cells are colored by sample labels (left) and cell types (right). (d) The UMAP plot of all scATAC-seq data collected from retina. Cells are colored by well-positioned-cPeak ratios.

Responses to Reviewer #2’s comments
The authors have addressed most of our comments. One minor issue remains: Reviewer 1’s question concerns unobserved cell types—i.e., cases with zero abundance in the training data. In that setting, how can cPeaks serve as a valid peak list for that cell type? The hold-out (masked) evaluation in Fig. 2c helps address this and should be emphasized. However, the newly added sentence “cPeaks are constructed across a wide range of tissues and cell types, independent of their prevalence in any single dataset…” is misleading. “Independent” is ambiguous and overstates the claim. We understand the intent is to say that aggregating across datasets reduces prevalence-driven filtering (so rare-accessible loci are less likely to be lost), not that cPeaks are statistically independent of training composition.
Reponses:
Thank you for the helpful feedback. We agree with your point regarding the ambiguity of the term “independent.” We have revised the sentence in Line 429 to read: “cPeaks are constructed across a wide range of tissues and cell types, and their composition is not dominated by the prevalence of any single dataset.” This change more accurately reflects our intended meaning.
